Carboxylic Acid. An organic functional group characterized by a carbon atom double-bonded to an oxygen and single-bonded to a hydroxyl group, represented as COOH. Because both the carbonyl and the hydroxyl components are polar, carboxylic acids can form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds. This gives them significantly higher boiling points than comparable hydrocarbons. They're weak acids that partially dissociate in aqueous solution to yield a resonance-stabilized carboxylate anion and a hydronium ion. Carboxylic acids are ubiquitous in biology, forming the building blocks of amino acids, fatty acids, and many metabolic intermediates.

The carboxyl group combines a polar carbonyl with a polar hydroxyl on a single carbon. In the gas phase and in nonpolar solvents, carboxylic acids form stable hydrogen-bonded dimers, which substantially elevates their boiling and melting points relative to their molecular weight. They display weak acidity in water, typically exhibiting pKa values between three and five, due to resonance stabilization of the negative charge across both oxygen atoms in the carboxylate conjugate base.

Carboxylic acids are prepared by oxidizing primary alcohols or aldehydes using strong oxidizing agents like potassium permanganate or chromic acid. They react with alcohols in Fischer esterification under acid catalysis to produce esters and water. That's a reversible equilibrium reaction. With amines under heat or using coupling reagents like DCC, they synthesize amides, which constitute the peptide bonds in proteins. When heated, carboxylic acids undergo decarboxylation, especially beta-keto acids, releasing carbon dioxide gas and forming a simplified hydrocarbon. They can be reduced to primary alcohols using lithium aluminum hydride, though they're resistant to milder reducing agents like sodium borohydride.

Carboxylic acids are the primary acidic functional group in organic chemistry, serving as precursors to esters, amides, and acid anhydrides. They're central to cellular metabolism, appearing in the citric acid cycle as intermediates like citric, succinic, and malic acids. Reacting a carboxylic acid with an alcohol forms an ester. With an amine, it forms an amide. Primary alcohols oxidize to yield carboxylic acids. And the two oxygen atoms in the carboxyl group carry the partial charges that enable hydrogen bonding and resonance.
